questions.q: Collect five numbers into a list and print the list.
brief: Read five whole numbers, one on each line.
Put them in a list, in the order they are typed.
Print the list itself, the way Python prints a list - for example: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
questions.starter:
nums = []

# Read five whole numbers into nums, then print nums

tests.why: The list has to keep the order the numbers were typed in.
Repeats are allowed - a list keeps every item, even when two are the same.
If you got ['30', '5', '100', '5', '12'] with quote marks you stored the text from input() instead of turning it into a number with int().

questions.fb: Start with an empty list and .append() each number as you read it - printing the list shows the square brackets and commas for you.

questions.q: Read some colours into a list, then print how many and the last one.
brief: Read one whole number saying how many colours follow.
Read that many colours, one on each line, into a list.
Print how many colours are in the list.
Print the last colour in the list on the next line.
questions.starter: # Read the count, then read that many colours into a list

tests.why: len() counts the items; the last one is at position len - 1, not len.
With one colour the first item is also the last - colours[1] is already past the end of the list.
The count must come from len(), not from printing the number you read at the start - they only match if every colour was appended.

questions.fb: len(list) tells you how many items there are, so the highest position you can read is len(list) - 1.

questions.q: Print the lunch at the position typed in.
brief: The list is written for you - do not change it.
Read one whole number. It is a position in the list, counting from 0.
Print the item at that position, and nothing else.
questions.starter:
lunches = ['tomato soup', 'veg curry', 'fish pie', 'jacket potato', 'pasta bake', 'bean chilli']

# Read a position and print the lunch at that position

tests.why: Position 0 is the first item. If you printed 'bean chilli' you used lunches[p - 1], and with p = 0 that counts backwards from the end.
Position 3 is the fourth item, because the counting starts at 0.
There are six items, so the last position is 5 - adding 1 here would run off the end of the list.
Position 1 is the second item, not the first.

questions.fb: A list of six items has positions 0 to 5 - the last position is always one less than the length.

questions.q: Print the scores at two positions in the list, then their total.
brief: The list is written for you - do not change it.
Read two whole numbers, each a position counting from 0: the first position, then the second.
Print the score at the first position.
Print the score at the second position on the next line.
Print the two scores added together on the line after that.
questions.starter:
scores = [14, 9, 22, 5, 17, 30, 8]

# Read two positions, print both scores and their total

tests.why: 0 is the first score and 6 is the last of seven - if either came out wrong you are counting from 1.
Read the positions in the order the brief gives them - swapping them swaps the first two lines.
The same position twice is allowed - the score is simply used twice, so the total is double it.
Add the two scores you looked up, not the two position numbers.

questions.fb: Looking an item up with scores[a] gives you a number you can use in a sum like any other.

questions.q: Print each of four plant names with how many letters it has.
brief: Read four plant names, one on each line, into a list.
Go through the list with a for loop.
For each plant print its name, a single space, then how many letters it has.
One line for each plant, in the order they were typed.
questions.starter:
plants = []

# Read four names, then loop through the list printing each name and its length

tests.why: One line per plant, name first and length second, in the typed order.
Four lines even when every length is the same - the loop must run once for every item.
If you only got one line you printed after the loop instead of inside it - check the indentation.

questions.fb: A for loop over a list hands you the items one at a time, so you never need a position number for this job.

questions.q: Print each of five numbers next to the position it is stored at.
brief: Read five whole numbers, one on each line, into a list.
Go through the positions of the list using range(len(...)).
For each position print the position number, a single space, then the number stored there.
Positions count from 0.
questions.starter:
nums = []

# Read five numbers, then loop over the positions with range(len(nums))

tests.why: The first line must be 0 7. If it says 1 7 you started counting the positions at 1.
With all five numbers the same, only the positions change - this is the clearest check that they run 0 to 4.
range(len(nums)) gives 0 up to 4 for five items - range(1, len(nums)) would miss the first one.

questions.fb: range(len(nums)) counts the positions, so nums[i] is the item at the position the loop is on.

questions.q: Add two items to the basket, then list the whole basket.
brief: The four items already in the list are written for you - do not change them.
Read two more items, one on each line, and add each one to the end of the list with .append().
Print how many items are in the list.
Then print every item on its own line, in order.
questions.starter:
basket = ['apple', 'pear', 'plum', 'grape']

# Read two more items, append them, then print the count and the whole basket

tests.why: .append() puts an item on the end, so the two new ones come after grape in the order they were typed.
The count comes from len() after both appends - four plus two is six, not four.
If an item is missing you may have replaced the list with the new value instead of appending to it.

questions.fb: basket.append(x) changes the list you already have - it does not make a new one, so there is nothing to assign.

questions.q: Remove a named person from the queue, then the one at a given position.
brief: The queue is written for you - do not change it.
Read one name, then read one whole number.
First take the named person out of the list using .remove().
Then, working on the list as it now is, delete the person at the position given by the number, using del. Positions count from 0.
Print the names that are left, one on each line, in order.
questions.starter:
queue = ['Ama', 'Bo', 'Cai', 'Dara', 'Esme', 'Finn']

# Remove the named person, then del the person at the given position, then print the rest

tests.why: Position 0 is the front of the list after Cai has gone, so Ama is the one deleted - if Bo disappeared you counted from 1.
The position is read against the shortened list. Deleting from the original six would have taken Dara instead of Esme.
Five names are left after the remove, so 4 is the last position - this is where going one too far crashes the program.
.remove() takes a name, del takes a position - mixing them up is the usual slip here.

questions.fb: .remove() is given the value to take out; del is given the position - and each one makes the list shorter straight away.

questions.q: Total five numbers and work out their average.
brief: Read five whole numbers, one on each line, into a list.
Print the total of the five numbers.
Print the average on the next line, rounded to one decimal place.
A whole average still shows one decimal place - 5 is printed as 5.0
questions.starter:
nums = []

# Read five numbers, add them up with a loop, then print the total and the average

tests.why: The average is the total divided by how many numbers there are. It must show one decimal place, so 5.0 and not 5.
Round to one decimal place with round(total / 5, 1) - printing the raw division gives 10.2 here but a long run of digits for other data.
If the total is right but the average is not, check you divided by 5 and not by 4.
All zeros should still work - a running total that starts at 0 handles this, one that starts at the first number does too, but one that starts at 1 does not.

questions.fb: Start the running total at 0 before the loop, add each item inside the loop, and divide only once the loop has finished.

questions.q: Find the largest and smallest of seven numbers without max() or min().
brief: Read seven whole numbers, one on each line, into a list.
Find the largest and the smallest yourself, with a loop.
Print the largest.
Print the smallest on the next line.
Do not use max() or min().
questions.starter:
nums = []

# Read seven numbers, then find the largest and smallest with a loop

tests.why: Largest first, smallest second - printing them the other way round is the easiest mark to lose here.
When every number is the same it is both the largest and the smallest, so your comparisons must use > and < and not >= and <= in a way that breaks.
All seven are negative. Starting largest at 0 would wrongly report 0, so start it at the first item in the list instead.
The largest and the smallest are both near the start - a loop that begins at position 1 would skip the 50 entirely.

questions.fb: Start both answers at the first item, then compare every item against them in turn - the first item is the only safe starting guess.
forbid: The point of this question is the loop - find the largest yourself rather than using max().
The point of this question is the loop - find the smallest yourself rather than using min().

questions.q: Report on eight quiz marks: total, average, passes and where the best is.
brief: Read eight whole numbers, one on each line, into a list. Each one is a mark out of 20.
Print the total of the eight marks.
Print the average on the next line, rounded to one decimal place. A whole average still shows one decimal place - 13 is printed as 13.0
Print how many of the marks are 12 or more on the line after that.
Print the position of the highest mark on the last line, counting from 0. If two marks are equally high, give the position of the first one.
Do not use max() or .index() - find the highest mark with a loop.
questions.starter:
marks = []

# Read eight marks, then print the total, the average, the number of passes
# and the position of the highest mark

tests.why: Four lines in the order the brief gives. The highest mark 20 is the third one, which is position 2 - position 3 means you counted from 1.
Nothing reaches 12, so the count of passes is 0 - a counter must start at 0 and be printed even when nothing was counted.
Two marks are 20. The brief asks for the first of them, position 1, so compare with > and not >= when you update the best position.
A mark of exactly 12 counts as a pass, so the answer is 4 - if you got 0 you used > 12 instead of >= 12.
The highest mark is the very last one, position 7 - a loop that stops one short of the end never sees it.

questions.fb: Four separate jobs over the same list: one running total, one counter with a condition, and one remembered position that you keep updating.
forbid: Find the highest mark with a loop of your own rather than using max().
Find the position of the highest mark as you go rather than looking it up with .index().
